title: A prisoner’s cry is answered with peace and limits on priesthood power
setting: Joseph Smith wrote this from the jail at Liberty, Clay County, Missouri, in March 1839. He, Hyrum Smith, Lyman Wight, Caleb Baldwin, and Alexander McRae had been held there since 1 December 1838. They awaited trial on charges from the 1838 conflict in Missouri. Governor Lilburn Boggs had ordered the Saints out of the state, and most had fled to Illinois. Appeals to officials had brought no relief. The section joins passages from two letters to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church, dated 20 March and about 22 March.
summary: The section opens with a prayer: “O God, where art thou?” Joseph asks how long the Saints must suffer and pleads for God to act. A reply then speaks to him as “my son” and promises peace. His trial will be “but a small moment,” and his friends still stand by him. The text warns those who falsely accuse the Saints, drive them, and kill them. It promises knowledge by the Holy Ghost that has not been revealed before. It says many are called but few chosen, because they seek worldly honors. Priesthood power, it says, rests only on persuasion, patience, gentleness, meekness, kindness, and unfeigned love.

contextNote.title: Why priesthood cannot be forced
contextNote.text: Verse 39 states the problem: people who get “a little authority” soon practice “unrighteous dominion”. Verse 36 explains why that fails, because priesthood rights are tied to “the powers of heaven”. Verse 37 adds that when someone uses compulsion, “the heavens withdraw themselves”. Verse 41 then lists the only means that keep priesthood influence: persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, meekness, and unfeigned love. Joseph wrote this while he himself was held by force. In this passage, power means influence earned by love, not control taken by pressure.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 121–123 takes its title from verse 1. It links Joseph’s prayer in verses 1–6 to the answer of peace in verses 7–8. Which qualities in verses 41–45 describe how you could use any influence you hold at home or at church?

jsp.title: Letter to the Church and Edward Partridge, 20 March 1839

reviewNote: Read all 46 verses. Official heading: prayer and prophecies from two epistles written in Liberty jail, the first dated 20 March 1839, the second about 22 March. JSP historical introductions read for both letters (the second is 'Letter to Edward Partridge and the Church, circa 22 March 1839', https://www.josephsmithpapers.org/paper-summary/letter-to-edward-partridge-and-the-church-circa-22-march-1839): confinement from 1 December 1838, fellow prisoners, letters sent to Emma Smith in Quincy, prisoners leaving the jail 6 April 1839. Sidney Rigdon was also jailed but released earlier and is not listed. The exact verse split between the two letters was not confirmed, so the text does not assign verses to letters. Boggs's order date comes from the D&C 124 heading.
